topic.name: Writing the Vector Equation of a Line Using the Cross Product

exampleAnswers.title: Converting Between Vector and Cross Product Form for a Given Straight Line

question.text: Write the vector equation of the line \[ \left(\mathbf{r}- \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 4\\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -6 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \] in the form $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}$, $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$
question.explanation:
The equation of the line using the cross product takes the general form \[ (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}. \]

Comparing this general form to the given equation, we find that

  • the vector $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\-6 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix}$ is parallel to the line, and

  • $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 4 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of the point $P(-5,4,-4)$ that lies on the line.

Therefore, the given vector equation can be written as \[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 4 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -6 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty). \]

example.title: Converting Between Vector and Cross Product Form for a Given Straight Line

question.text: The vector equation of a straight line is given by \[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \\ -10 \end{bmatrix}, \] for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the vector equation of the line in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$
question.explanation:
The general form of the vector equation for a line is \[ \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}t, \] and comparing this general form to our equation above, we find that

  • $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of the point $P(2,0,5)$ that lies on the line, and

  • the vector $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \\ -10 \end{bmatrix}$ is parallel to the line.

Therefore, the cross product equation for the line is

\[ \left( \mathbf{r} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \\ -10 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}. \]

question.text: The canonical equation of the line is given by $ \dfrac{x-2}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{-2}=\dfrac{z-1}{-2}. $ Find the vector equation of this line in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$
question.explanation:
Looking at the denominators of the canonical equation, we find that the direction vector is $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}.$

We also have the position vector $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ for the point $P(2,2,1)$ that lies on the line.

Therefore, the equation can be written as \[ \left( \mathbf{r} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Converting Between Parametric and Cross Product Form for a Given Straight Line

question.text: The parametric equations of a straight line are given by \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} x = 1+3t \\ y = 3+7t \\ z = 8-6t, \end{array} \right. \] for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the vector equation of the line in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$
question.explanation:
The corresponding vector equation is given by \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1+3t \\ 3+7t \\ 8-6t \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 3t \\ 7t \\ -6t \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*}

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

The general form of the vector equation for a line is \[ \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}t, \] and comparing this general form to our equation above, we find that

  • $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of the point $P(1,3,8)$ that lies on the line, and

  • the vector $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}$ is parallel to the line.

Therefore, the cross product equation for the line is

\[ \left( \mathbf{r} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}. \]

example.title: Converting Between Parametric and Cross Product Form for a Given Straight Line

question.text: The vector equation of a line is given by \[ \left( \mathbf{r} - \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}. \] Find its parametric equations.
question.explanation:
The equation of the line using the cross product takes the general form \[ (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}. \]

Comparing this general form to the given equation, we find that

  • the vector $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$ is parallel to the line, and

  • $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of the point $P(-8,2,3)$ that lies on the line.

Therefore, the given vector equation can be written as \begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}\\ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -2t \\ 0 \\ -3t \end{bmatrix}\\ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -8 -2t \\ 2 \\ 3-3t \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*}

and finally, the parametric equations are \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} x = -8-2t \\ y = 2 \\ z = 3-3t \end{array} \right. \] where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Cross Product Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points

question.text: A line passes through the points $P(1,-1,-4)$ and $Q(2,7,-3).$ Find its vector equation in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$
question.explanation:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(1,-1,-4)$ and $Q(2,7,-3).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \overrightarrow{PQ} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 7 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, to get the equation of the line using the cross product, we substitute in our values of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as follows:

\[ \left( \mathbf{r} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \right) \times \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}. \]

example.title: Finding the Cross Product Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points

question.text: A line passes through the points $P(-3,-1,4)$ and $Q(1,8,9).$ Find its vector equation in the form $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c}.$
question.explanation:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-3,-1,4)$ and $Q(1,8,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \overrightarrow{PQ} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 8 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \left( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p} \right) \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{v} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -3 & -1 & 4\\ 4 & 9 & 5 \end{array} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} &= -41\mathbf{i}-31\mathbf{j}+23\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

question.text: A line passes through the points $P(6,3,1)$ and $Q(2,4,9).$ Find its vector equation in the form $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c}.$
question.explanation:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(6,3,1)$ and $Q(2,4,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{v} &= \overrightarrow{PQ} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \left( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p} \right) \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{v} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 6 & 3 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8 \end{array} \\[5pt] \mathbf{r} \times \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} &= 23\mathbf{i}-52\mathbf{j}+18\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}
